extracted.intended_audience: agency rulemaking officials, eRulemaking Project Management Office (eRulemaking PMO), and other government actors involved in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Recommendations and best practices for how agencies and the eRulemaking PMO should manage, solicit, post, and respond to public comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking to promote participation and improve rulemaking outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish guidance on types of beneficial comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The eRulemaking Project Management Office should consider publishing a document explaining what types of comments are most beneficial and listing best practices for parties submitting comments. Individual agencies may publish supplements to the common document describing the qualities of effective comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once developed, these documents should be made publicly available by posting on the agency website, Regulations.gov, and any other venue that will promote widespread availability of the information. Purpose: promote optimal public participation and enhance the usefulness of public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set comment periods mindful of participation and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should set comment periods that consider the competing interests of promoting optimal public participation while ensuring that the rulemaking is conducted efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general matter, for 'significant regulatory action[s]' as defined in Executive Order 12,866, agencies should use a comment period of at least 60 days. For all other rulemakings, they should generally use a comment period of at least 30 days. When agencies set shorter comment periods in appropriate circumstances, they are encouraged to provide an appropriate explanation for doing so. (See related Executive Order guidance and prior ACUS recommendations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Post public comments to the Internet within a specified period
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt stated policies of posting public comments to the Internet within a specified period after submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should post all electronically submitted comments on the Internet and should also scan and post all comments submitted in paper format. See OMB expectations that agencies post public comments to Regulations.gov in a timely manner regardless of submission method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish and publish anonymous comment policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The eRulemaking Project Management Office and individual agencies should establish and publish policies regarding the submission of anonymous comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should clarify when anonymous submissions will be accepted, how they will be treated, and any limitations on their use in the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and publish policies on late comments and apply consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt and publish policies on late comments and should apply those policies consistently within each rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should determine whether or not they will accept late submissions in a given rulemaking and should announce the policy both in publicly accessible forums (e.g., the agency’s website, Regulations.gov) and in Federal Register notices including requests for comments. The agency may make clear that late comments are disfavored and will only be considered to the extent practicable. Example: DOT notice stating late comments will be included and considered to extent practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunities for reply comments or other input on submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, agencies should make use of reply comment periods or other opportunities for receiving public input on submitted comments, after all comments have been posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An opportunity for public input on submitted comments can entail a reply period for written comments on submitted comments, an oral hearing, or some other means for input on comments received. Prior ACUS recommendations and Executive Branch guidance support providing opportunities for parties to react to and benefit from others' comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor dockets and refresh the record when it becomes stale
rubrics_metrics.description: Although agencies should not automatically deem rulemaking comments to have become stale after any fixed period of time, agencies should closely monitor their rulemaking dockets and consider when the record has become stale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an agency believes the circumstances surrounding the rulemaking have materially changed or the rulemaking record has otherwise become stale, it should consider use of available mechanisms such as supplemental notices of proposed rulemaking to refresh the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor implementation to agency context and evaluate effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Different agencies have different approaches to rulemaking and therefore individual agencies should decide whether and how to implement the best practices addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Conference recommends that agencies and the Conference itself conduct further empirical analysis of notice-and-comment rulemaking, study effects of implemented recommendations, and adjust and build upon proposed processes as appropriate.
